bridge: Builds on N05 names and N04 byte streams. Inspect the supplied HTTP transcript before using developer tools.
teaching:
Imagine clicking “show my notes”. The browser sends a request describing what it wants; the server sends a response with a result. In the supplied transcript, GET is the method, /notes is the target path and Host identifies the requested host. Header lines carry named metadata in name: value form. A blank line separates headers from any message body. The JSON {"notes":[]} is response content: an empty list of notes, not a command for the browser to execute.

Stateless means HTTP itself does not automatically remember that two separate requests belong to one continuing user interaction. An application can add a session, meaning stored context for that interaction. A cookie is name/value data a browser may send on later eligible requests. Here session=DEMO_ONLY is an invented session credential. The application must validate it; a cookie being present does not prove the sender is authorised.

HTTP separates a request method and target from headers and optional content. A response carries a status, headers and optional content. Header names and their semantics matter: a 200 response indicates an application response, not a security approval.

Cookies connect later requests with stored state. The server sets a cookie, and the browser decides when to send it under domain, path, Secure, SameSite and other rules. HttpOnly restricts script access to a cookie; it does not stop the browser from sending it with eligible requests. A session identifier should be treated as a credential.

Caches reuse responses under defined policy. Shared caches and private browser caches have different users and trust boundaries. A proxy can terminate one connection and make another, so the application must know which forwarding metadata it can trust. Do not assume a user-supplied forwarded header is authoritative just because it names an IP address.

Client and server describe roles in an exchange. A reverse proxy can receive a browser request as a server and make an upstream request as a client; a service can perform both roles. Hostnames can resolve to changing or multiple server addresses, and a well-known port is a convention rather than proof of service identity.

The video’s readable request lines illustrate HTTP/1.1. HTTP/2 carries messages using binary frames over TCP, and HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics onto QUIC over UDP. The text transcript above is a teaching representation rather than the HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 wire format. Reusing a connection avoids repeated setup; first connections, TLS, response sizes, parallel requests and congestion still affect total latency. Ordinary TCP supplies neither encryption nor peer authentication. HTTPS adds a configured secure transport; certificate validation and application authorisation remain different checks.

HTTP being stateless does not forbid a server-side session. A cookie is name/value data, not necessarily a number. Set-Cookie delivers it to a browser; a later Cookie request header can carry it back when browser rules permit. The numeric shopping example is illustrative; do not assume every cookie identifies an authenticated person or that every server records a complete history. HttpOnly restricts script access but does not make all requests trustworthy.

Cache-Control: no-cache normally permits storage but requires successful validation before reuse; no-store forbids storage by compliant caches. private prevents shared-cache storage, while public can explicitly allow shared caching. Validators describe a representation: reuse an ETag in If-None-Match, or the server’s Last-Modified timestamp in If-Modified-Since, rather than substituting your local download time. For an applicable cached GET, 304 carries no replacement content and tells the cache to reuse/update its stored response metadata; a changed successful GET normally returns 200 with content. Cache keys and Vary matter, and a cache hit is not automatically safe for personalised data.

Trace the two directions separately. Cookie travels from browser to server on a request. Set-Cookie travels from server to browser on a response and asks the browser to store or update a cookie according to its rules. Status 200 reports a successful response; it does not certify the permission check. Content-Type names the representation format. A cache is a stored response for possible reuse; private and no-store control different aspects of that reuse. For the exercise, identify these lines before reading the more detailed HTTP-version and cache-validation notes above.
example:
GET /notes HTTP/1.1
Host: notes.example
Cookie: session=DEMO_ONLY

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: private, no-store
Set-Cookie: session=NEW_DEMO; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

{"notes":[]}

These are fictional credentials; never paste a real cookie into notes.
explanation: The browser sends a Cookie header in the request; the server sends Set-Cookie in the response. Secure restricts the cookie to secure transport in normal browser handling. no-store tells compliant caches not to store the response, while private excludes shared-cache storage when caching would otherwise be permitted. These flags address different mechanisms.
exercise: Annotate method, path, host, request credential, status, representation type and storage policy in the transcript. Explain what changes when the cookie is absent and why the answer depends on application policy rather than HTTP alone.
solution: The first line supplies method GET and path /notes. Host supplies notes.example. Cookie carries the invented session value used as a credential in this application. The response line reports status 200; Content-Type identifies JSON, and Cache-Control says private, no-store. Set-Cookie requests a new cookie with its listed attributes. If the request has no session cookie, the application might reject it, redirect to sign-in or provide a deliberately public response: HTTP alone does not choose. For protected notes, its authorisation policy must prevent an unauthenticated caller from receiving private content.
challenge: A response contains private user notes and Cache-Control: public,max-age=600. Explain the risk in a shared cache, propose a safer policy and give one verification case involving two invented users.
challenge_solution: Public storage can reuse a private representation across users if cache keys/policy permit it. Use a deliberate private/no-store policy for sensitive content and verify that user B never receives user A's response. Cookie flags alone do not fix shared response caching.
